stem: Neha starts at her office O and walks 10 km North to point A. From A she walks 6 km East to point B. From B she walks 10 km South to point C. What is the straight-line distance from O to C, and in which direction does C lie from O?

per_option_rationale.rationale: O=(0,0). A=(0,10). B=(6,10). C=(6,0). Distance OC = 6 km. C is due East of O since both have y=0 but C has x=6.
Treating the East walk as West (reversing the direction) places C at (-6,0), making C 6 km West of O.

The North (10) and South (10) legs do not cancel in this computation; instead only the last two legs (6 East, 10 South) are combined as a hypotenuse: sqrt(6^2+10^2) ~ 11.7, roughly approximated as 10 km South-East.
Adding the North and South distances (10+10=20) and the East distance (6) arithmetically gives 16, placed South-East by misidentifying the direction.

explanation: Track coordinates: O=(0,0), North 10 -> A=(0,10), East 6 -> B=(6,10), South 10 -> C=(6,0). The North and South legs are equal and cancel vertically. C is at (6,0), which is 6 km due East of O.

explanation_sections.punchline: Equal North and South legs cancel; only the East leg creates net displacement.
explanation_sections.approach: Apply clues most-certain-first: assign coordinates step by step. North adds +y, East adds +x, South subtracts y. O=(0,0)->A=(0,10)->B=(6,10)->C=(6,0). |OC|=6, direction = East (same latitude, positive x).
explanation_sections.lesson: Cancel opposite legs first; then identify direction from net x and y components.
explanation_sections.timing: About 70-80 seconds. The main trap is combining the last two legs into a hypotenuse instead of recognizing the cancellation.
